paragraphs.source_en: Justin I had demonstrated that most of the eastern Church (except Egypt) could be brought to heel by the court and dissenters could be persecuted. When Justinian came to power in 527, he relaxed the persecution of the monks, pos- sibly influenced by Theodora, who, it was said, leaned toward Monophysitism.48 But some Monophysites decided that the only way out of their predicament was to create a Church of their own. The step of ordaining separate Monophysite priests by the hundreds was taken by Yuhannan (John) of Tella in or before 530, while he was in hiding in the mountains, and he did so with permission from Severos of Antioch; one of the deacons that he created was the later Monophysite leader and historian John of Ephesos.49 This move frightened the court.

paragraphs.source_en: For both sides, the conditions of union were maximalist: “You have to admit that I am right and you are wrong; you have to rewrite the history of the past century; you have to erase your religious identity and replace it with ours; and then you have to beg forgiveness and, if we are feeling tolerant, we will allow you into the true Church.” This politics of maximum humiliation and zero concessions had been established by pope Hormisdas as the standard for “victory” in Church pol- itics. But the emperor needed to prevent the creation of a separate Church and was treating this as a schism, not heresy.
